video_title: If UPI Is Free, Who Pays for It? | PhonePe, Razorpay & NPCI | WTF is Payments?
gist: Four-and-a-half-hour roundtable with Nikhil Kamath, PhonePe CEO Sameer Nigam, Razorpay co-founder Harshil Mathur and NPCI growth ED Sohini dissecting UPI and card economics (who pays the ~25 bps UPI cost, the 1.85% card MDR stack), the zero-MDR and 30% market-cap fights, and India's over-regulation problem. It closes with views on CBDCs vs stablecoins, agentic payments (NPCI planning agentic UPI), the AI bubble, and Kamath's contrarian buys (Infosys/IT services, hotels, BookMyShow, energy storage), plus short cross-border/wearable founder segments.

themes.theme: UPI plumbing and who pays for 'free'

insights.claim: UPI processes roughly 783 million transactions a day (close to a billion including everything), and NPCI, a not-for-profit Section 8 company seeded with Rs 100 crore by ten banks, has self-funded all growth from surplus without paying dividends to its bank and fintech shareholders.
insights.speaker: Sohini (NPCI)
insights.so_what: UPI's core rail is a non-profit utility, so private monetisation has to come from apps, PSP banks and MDR rather than the switch.
insights.quote: Yes, so 783 million yesterday.

insights.claim: A single P2P UPI transfer involves roughly seven actors (app/TPAP, PSP sponsor bank, NPCI, issuer bank, beneficiary bank, VPA resolution) and about 10 API calls, at an estimated ecosystem-wide cost of about 25 basis points.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam / Sohini
insights.so_what: 'Free' UPI has a real cost borne by banks and apps, which is the economic basis for the MDR debate.
insights.quote: So, each transaction is roughly 10 API calls.

insights.claim: On a P2P UPI transfer the remitter's issuing bank pays the app's PSP bank a slab-based fee of roughly 15 to 50 paise, which PhonePe shares, justified as a saving versus branch, ATM and NEFT servicing costs (NEFT also costs banks 50 paise).
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: PSP-bank fees are the thin existing revenue line for UPI apps absent MDR.

insights.claim: PhonePe runs about 30,000 servers, claims the second-largest data footprint in India after the Jio group, and employs roughly 1,500-1,800 engineers on fraud, risk and settlement for UPI.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: Running a top UPI app is capital- and engineering-intensive despite zero consumer pricing.
insights.quote: We have about 30,000 servers now.

insights.claim: NPCI settles UPI ten times a day on a net basis through RTGS accounts at RBI, so 100 million peak-hour transactions collapse into roughly 800 gross settlement entries, and no intermediary holds float as in wallet-based Alipay/WeChat.
insights.speaker: Sohini (NPCI) / Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: Ledger-based real-time payments with deferred net settlement is why UPI scales cheaply, but also why there is no float income for apps.
insights.quote: We settle ten times a day.

insights.claim: The regulator backed UPI because Nandan Nilekani's camp warned that if India went digital on cards, Visa and Mastercard would take a monopoly worth about 50 basis points of GDP; the core build team was only about 20 people (Nilekani, Sharad Sharma, Pramod Jain, Sanjay Gupta, Dilip Asbe and others).
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: UPI was a sovereign-rails decision, which explains policy hostility to card-network economics.
insights.quote: Visa and Mastercard will have a monopoly on and 50 basis points of the GDP.

insights.claim: UPI's monthly volume runs about Rs 29.33 lakh crore (about a lakh crore a day), meaning annual UPI TPV now exceeds one turn of GDP, while retail B2C payments are typically only 1.2-1.3x GDP, so UPI is close to capturing most retail spending.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: Remaining UPI growth must come from B2B, government and larger-ticket flows rather than retail substitution.

insights.claim: RBI estimates 60% of household consumption spending is still cash (versus 80% three years earlier), whereas in the pre-UPI cards era only about 3% of personal consumption expenditure was digital.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Kamath / Sohini (NPCI)
insights.so_what: Digital share of consumption has inflected sharply but large cash pools (rent, property, B2B) remain.

insights.claim: On a credit-card transaction Razorpay charges a large merchant like Amazon about 1.85%, pays about 1.75% downstream and keeps about 10 bps, with roughly 1.45% going to the issuing bank to fund cost of credit and rewards; Visa/Mastercard take far less than the commonly assumed 2%.
insights.speaker: Harshil Mathur
insights.so_what: Payment-gateway margins are razor thin; the issuer, not the network, captures most of the MDR.
insights.quote: So, I'll make 10 basis points.

insights.claim: Payment gateways price ad valorem rather than flat because they underwrite merchant-default risk: if a merchant takes payments and disappears, the acquirer/aggregator is liable for chargebacks.
insights.speaker: Harshil Mathur
insights.so_what: Merchant underwriting is the real moat and cost centre of PGs, not the switching.
insights.quote: The percentage based is because I am essentially underwriting a risk.

insights.claim: For online merchants cash-on-delivery costs about 5% once fraud, logistics and returns are counted, which is higher than a 1.75% card MDR, so charging MDR on online UPI would not push merchants back to cash.
insights.speaker: Harshil Mathur
insights.so_what: The online MDR case differs from offline kiranas; policy should segment by use case.
insights.quote: COD is 5%.

insights.claim: The US has high card success rates but 100-200 bps fraud because it lacks two-factor authentication, while India's mandated 2FA/OTP crushed consumer-side fraud but raised failure rates; Razorpay's edge was engineering higher success rates across the chain.
insights.speaker: Harshil Mathur
insights.so_what: In India, payment success rate is the key competitive metric for online gateways.

insights.claim: During Flipkart's first Big Billion Day sale, about 10 million card payment attempts in eight hours saw roughly 9 million fail, core banking systems of several banks including SBI went down, and 35,000-40,000 TVs were sold on 'failed' transactions later deemed successful.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: Legacy card and bank stacks were not built for Indian peak scale, which created the opening for UPI.
insights.quote: I remember we drove about 10 million credit card and debit card payment attempts in a eight-hour window, 9 million of them failed.

insights.claim: Urban Indians under 30 average two credit cards, and the majority of those are RuPay cards because RuPay credit works on UPI QR acceptance, which Visa and Mastercard cards cannot.
insights.speaker: Harshil Mathur / Sohini (NPCI)
insights.so_what: RuPay-on-UPI is quietly shifting young credit users away from the global networks.
insights.quote: majority of those cards under 30 are actually RuPay cards today

insights.claim: Acquirer-side price cuts do not drive card usage because consumers choose the instrument; issuers instead pass margin back as cashback and reward multipliers, often co-funded with platforms during sales.
insights.speaker: Harshil Mathur
insights.so_what: A new bank trying to win share via cheaper MDR would fail; consumer incentives are the lever.
insights.quote: acquiring cost doesn't drive consumer behaviour

themes.theme: Zero MDR, market-share caps and fear of big

insights.claim: Since zero MDR, around a hundred UPI third-party apps, including Tata and Ambani-backed entries, have entered and exited because there is no money in the category, which Nigam argues disincentivises the private sector that makes UPI work.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: Reintroducing MDR would change the economics of UPI incumbents like PhonePe; Nigam says he is grateful the government is looking at bringing it back.
insights.quote: a hundred TPAPs have come and gone in the last six years

insights.claim: Sameer Nigam opposes the proposed 30% UPI app market-share cap, arguing that in an interoperable rail with NPCI-set pricing and no barrier to entry, a share cap is market manipulation rather than risk mitigation, comparable to forcing WhatsApp users onto Telegram.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: The cap is a live regulatory overhang on PhonePe's growth and IPO narrative.

insights.claim: Harshil Mathur and Nikhil Kamath counter that some intervention is inevitable once a player approaches 80-90% share, citing the Durbin Amendment in US acquiring and Zerodha's own 15% cap on derivatives open interest, which forced it to restrict far out-of-the-money strikes and lose clients to smaller brokers.
insights.speaker: Harshil Mathur / Nikhil Kamath
insights.so_what: Indian market structure regulation tends to cap leaders' features rather than ban growth outright.
insights.quote: We hit the 15% cap.

insights.claim: Nigam says PhonePe's insurance revenue is about a twentieth of Policybazaar's despite PhonePe having roughly 50x the distribution base, undercutting the assumption that a large payments platform automatically dominates cross-sell.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: Payments scale does not translate into financial-product share, weakening the anti-monopoly argument.

insights.claim: Alipay and WeChat Pay each separately process more transactions than NPCI, and China's PBOC responded with transaction-size caps on wallets rather than market-share caps.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam / Sohini (NPCI)
insights.so_what: UPI's global leadership claim is by real-time interoperable volume, not total digital payments.
insights.quote: Ali and WeChat separately process more transactions than NPCI today.

insights.claim: Regulators prefer supervising a few large players, which is why India has few new banks; there are about 1,300 banks but only about 35 universal banks and about 1,200 cooperative banks, and the licence itself is the biggest moat in banking.
insights.speaker: Harshil Mathur / Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: Digital-only banking licences (recommended by NITI Aayog) remain the key unlock for fintechs like PhonePe and Razorpay.
insights.quote: The banking, the single biggest moat in banking is the licence.

insights.claim: Payments banks failed because they could not lend and had a Rs 1 lakh deposit cap, whereas small finance banks worked better because they could lend; Airtel Payments Bank is the main survivor.
insights.speaker: Harshil Mathur / Sohini (NPCI)
insights.so_what: Any new licence category without lending economics is likely to fail.

insights.claim: The first mover in every Indian consumer category gets punished: Flipkart has faced an ED FEMA probe for about 15 years, and Karnataka's bike-taxi ban raised Outer Ring Road traffic about 35% overnight.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk is a persistent discount factor for Indian consumer-tech investors and FDI.
insights.quote: The first actor in every category gets burned in India.

insights.claim: In 1990 India's per-capita income (about $370) was slightly above China's (about $320) with equal GDP, and Nigam attributes China's divergence to eliminating fear via amnesty-style enforcement while India's 'process is the punishment'.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam / Nikhil Kamath
insights.so_what: Reducing regulatory fear and enforcing presumption of innocence is framed as the main growth lever.
insights.quote: The process is the punishment.

insights.claim: Harshil Mathur argues India executes centrally-run programmes well (UPI, vaccines) but fails at decentralised delivery, partly because states like Karnataka do not keep the upside of their own revenue growth, unlike Chinese provinces.
insights.speaker: Harshil Mathur
insights.so_what: Expect India's wins to keep coming from central digital public infrastructure rather than local execution.

themes.theme: Consumption data and the shape of Indian demand

insights.claim: Tier-2-and-below towns have consistently contributed 65-70% of digital consumer payments on UPI, with money moving village-to-village, not just metro-to-village remittances.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: Consumer demand is far deeper outside metros than e-commerce data suggests.

insights.claim: About 70% of online e-commerce spend by value comes from only about 15 million households, and grocery remains about 90% offline.
insights.speaker: Harshil Mathur
insights.so_what: Indian e-commerce TAM is narrow today, with roughly a five-year lag behind digital-payments adoption.
insights.quote: 70% of all online e-commerce purchases are done by 15 million users, 15 million households.

insights.claim: PhonePe's analysis of the recent GST rate changes, controlling for Diwali, found a roughly 2% GST cut produced a 5.5-6% consumption increase, a 5% cut produced about 13%, a 4-5% hike cut buying about 6%, and unchanged categories moved only about -0.2%.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: Indirect-tax cuts have high consumption elasticity, supportive of consumer-discretionary names after GST rationalisation.
insights.quote: GST went down in some categories by 5%, there was a 13% increase in buying.

insights.claim: Quick commerce has crossed 50% share in some metro districts and is decimating offline stores in dense clusters, but the phenomenon stops at about 10 cities; Nigam would still buy quick commerce at current valuations with Indian money.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: Quick commerce growth outside top cities will come as slotted/30-minute delivery rather than 10-minute.
insights.quote: But that phenomenon stops at 10 cities.

insights.claim: Assisted commerce dominates discretionary purchases: about 40-50% of travel is bought through agents and about 90% of insurance through offline brokers, while Meesho (claiming about 200 million yearly active users) remains about 90% cash-on-delivery due to trust.
insights.speaker: Harshil Mathur / Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: Vernacular AI agents and UPI escrow are the unlocks for tier-2+ e-commerce penetration.

insights.claim: Sameer Nigam proposes adding escrow to UPI online payments, with release triggered by a delivery OTP, as the feature that would kill cash-on-delivery for first-time buyers, mirroring PayPal-eBay.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: UPI escrow is a product opportunity for apps and PGs.
insights.quote: COD will go away if a UPI payment, for example, had escrow.

insights.claim: The panel argues India should shift to property and inheritance taxes (Nigam suggests starting at about 0.25% property tax) because black money flows into land and stamp duty distorts price discovery.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam / Nikhil Kamath
insights.so_what: A property tax would likely redirect household savings from real estate into equities.
insights.quote: All black money in India somehow finds its way into property.

insights.claim: B2B payments are the largest unsolved opportunity: a typical small retailer has 70-80 distributors paid Rs 1,500-50,000 weekly, and the problem is the workflow (invoice verification, reconciliation, TDS, GST filing) rather than the payment rail.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam / Harshil Mathur
insights.so_what: A 'UPI for business' SME finance app (aided by NPCI's new multi-signatory UPI) is an open startup lane.
insights.quote: B2B is a massive problem. Completely unsolved.

insights.claim: Sameer Nigam predicts that within ten years real-time payment networks peering with each other (UPI with Pix and others) will move faster than CBDCs for cross-border, and calls a domestic Indian CBDC a solution waiting for a problem.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: Bet on network-interlinking plays rather than CBDC infrastructure.
insights.quote: Real-time networks peering will move much faster than CBDCs.

insights.claim: Harshil Mathur argues stablecoins could be allowed in India if on-ramps and off-ramps are regulated like AD-III dealers/FFMCs with LRS limits, since stablecoin transfers are just ledger entries with no correspondent banks.
insights.speaker: Harshil Mathur
insights.so_what: Regulated ramps, not tokens, are where Indian stablecoin licensing would focus.
insights.quote: You have to separate the technology with the regulation.

insights.claim: Sohini says stablecoins have no off-ramp in India and she is not for it, while PayGlocal founders add RBI clearly prefers CBDC over stablecoins and see Project Nexus/BIS work as the cross-border path.
insights.speaker: Sohini (NPCI) / Prachi Dharani (PayGlocal)
insights.so_what: Indian stablecoin exposure stays a grey zone; regulated cross-border rails are the near-term opportunity.
insights.quote: Stablecoins have no off-ramp in India, right?

insights.claim: India receives about $125 billion of remittances per the World Bank, and Sohini sees an opportunity in inbound medical-tourism payments, mainly from the Middle East, where foreign patients' card transactions get declined by fraud models.
insights.speaker: Sohini (NPCI)
insights.so_what: Niche inbound cross-border corridors are underserved.
insights.quote: $125 billion is what the World Bank report says.

insights.claim: PayGlocal says cross-border card payment success rates in India were around 50-60% industry-wide and its orchestration lifts them to 80%+ (90%+ for some merchants), while UPI is now 80%+ of Indian consumer payments.
insights.speaker: Yogesh Lokhande (PayGlocal)
insights.so_what: Success-rate orchestration is the monetisable wedge in cross-border acceptance.

insights.claim: Seven's RuPay smart-ring economics: of about 1.6% card revenue, about 0.1% goes to the network and the remaining 1.5% splits about 70-30 between co-brand (1.1%) and PPI issuer LivQuik (0.4%), with Seven passing 1% back as cashback; NFC sound boxes could expand tap acceptance from about 1 crore to 4-5 crore touchpoints.
insights.speaker: Vijay Khubchandani (Seven)
insights.so_what: NFC acceptance build-out is the gating factor for wearable payments in India.

themes.theme: Agentic commerce, AI bubble and contrarian bets

insights.claim: NPCI is hoping to launch agentic payments on UPI at the Global Fintech Fest (9-11 September), building an interoperable framework so LLM platforms cannot strike bilateral exclusive payment deals.
insights.speaker: Sohini (NPCI)
insights.so_what: Agentic UPI would make India an early testbed for AI-agent payments on public rails.
insights.quote: this year, we are hoping to be able to launch the agentic payments on UPI.

insights.claim: Sameer Nigam says ChatGPT pulled back its Indian commerce experiments because token costs require a 13-14% margin per transaction, more than any commerce player earns; Harshil Mathur strongly disagrees, arguing token costs are trending to zero and open-source models are 10-20x cheaper.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam / Harshil Mathur
insights.so_what: Unit economics of chat-based commerce remain disputed; merchant-owned agents may come first.
insights.quote: the margin that they need per transaction, 13% to 14%, which is more than what any -commerce player can make.

insights.claim: Harshil Mathur argues agentic commerce will take off faster in India than the US because low e-commerce penetration means less channel conflict, and vernacular agents spanning 18 languages can replace assisted-commerce intermediaries; Nykaa and ixigo have already launched agents.
insights.speaker: Harshil Mathur
insights.so_what: Indian consumer platforms that build vernacular agents could expand their addressable market.

insights.claim: Sameer Nigam calls AI a bubble that will burst hard, while expecting AI itself to thrive over three to five years; he views Nvidia as 'the gangster in town' but flags its backstopping of GPU-backed debt and OpenAI as a risk, and says Microsoft has effectively thrown in the towel on owning a frontier destination.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: Expect a valuation reset in AI infrastructure names without a collapse in adoption.
insights.quote: I think the bubble's bursting hard.

insights.claim: Bangalore startups, including PhonePe and Razorpay, increasingly use Chinese open-source models for cost and control, and Mathur runs DeepSeek V4-Flash locally on an Nvidia DGX Spark (about Rs 5-6 lakh) for under Rs 1,000 a month in power.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam / Harshil Mathur
insights.so_what: Open-weight Chinese models are eroding frontier-lab pricing power in emerging-market enterprise use.
insights.quote: I have a DGX Spark running at my home on which I have a DeepSeek V4-Flash model.

insights.claim: Sameer Nigam argues AI's labour impact will be muted in India in the short run because displacing an engineering job removes about $10,000 versus $120,000 in the US, and humanity decides how to use foundational technology over an 8-10 year span.
insights.speaker: Sameer Nigam
insights.so_what: Indian IT and services labour arbitrage may persist longer than US-centric AI narratives suggest.

insights.claim: Harshil Mathur argues most AI value will accrue at the application/last-mile layer as with Google and Facebook after the PC era, with infrastructure 'shovels' like compressing company data into proprietary models (Razorpay's Vulcan) offering medium-risk returns.
insights.speaker: Harshil Mathur
insights.so_what: Application layer is winner-take-all and high-risk; enabling layers are the steadier bet.

insights.claim: Nikhil Kamath says he is making contrarian bets: buying Infosys and IT services at 12-13x PAT with about $6 billion cash and AI revenue up 8-9% this quarter, plus hotels, BookMyShow-style live events, travel and energy storage, while avoiding high-growth AI names.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Kamath
insights.so_what: A prominent Indian investor is positioning for an AI-productivity world via experiences and cheap IT services rather than AI multiples.
insights.quote: I'm buying IT services because I feel like a company like Infosys has $6 billion of cash, I'm paying a 12, 13 multiple on PAT.

insights.claim: Kamath recounts Sam Altman telling him to buy Louis Vuitton stock as a bet that AI productivity gains flow to status brands, noting LV is down about 30% for the year.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Kamath
insights.so_what: Luxury as an AI-wealth beneficiary is a thesis that has not yet paid off.
insights.quote: Buy Louis Vuitton stock.

insights.claim: Dodo Payments says its codebase went from about 20-30% AI-written two years ago to about 99.99% AI-written today, with engineers writing specs and reviewing; it advises against building agentic payments in India now because the wave is two to three years out.
insights.speaker: Ayush (Dodo Payments)
insights.so_what: Founders see agentic payments as premature in India despite NPCI's push.
